newsitem.title: USA: Candian National Railway party fuels rumors.
newsitem.headline: Candian National Railway party fuels rumors.

text.p: The guest list at a recent party thrown by Canadian National Railway Co. is fueling speculation that the company may be in talks to buy Illinois Central Corp..

The rumors come amid industry views that Illinois Central is increasingly vulnerable as a takeover target in a period of industrywide consolidation that includes the proposed $10.3 billion sale of Conrail Inc. to powerhouses CSX Corp. and Norfolk Southern Corp..

The most recent round of merger talk comes on the heels of a May 16 party hosted by Canadian National to celebrate its new intermodal (rail-and-truck shipments) facility at Harvey, Ill. The terminal is located on property owned by Illinois Central and also was built by the Chicago-based railroad.

Top executives of both railroads attended the party, leading to speculation that a merger may be in the works even though the two companies already have a relationship through a marketing agreement in which Illinois Central markets its services and route structures to Canadian National.
"I think it is only a matter of time before Illinois Central is acquired," said Steve Lewins of Gruntal & Co.
Over the past few weeks, merger speculation has propelled shares of Illinois Central to $36 per share from an April low of about $31.50.

It has been nearly three years since Illinois Central was prepared to participate in the industry consolidation with a plan to buy Kansas City Southern Industries Inc. for $686 million. The deal collapsed a few months later when the companies failed to agree on the terms of the transaction.

Illinois Central spokeswoman Ann Thoma said the company does not comment on speculation or rumors. She also noted that the railroad has similar agreements with other carriers, not just Canadian National.
"Our view is that we can be a very successful independent raiload with our own strategy," she said.

Canadian National also declined to comment on the rumors. In a speech at the terminal's official opening, Chief Executive Paul Tellier said the company's strategy includes tapping new markets and building alliances.

The merger talk has generated little enthusiasm among railroad experts, who said a potential union would result in few cost savings or advantages to the Canadian carrier, which already has coveted access to the U.S. Gulf through its existing arrangement with Illinois Central. U.S. Gulf access is important for exports of grain and other products.

"It's a nice initial step into the merger game. Everybody wants to be bigger in this business. But are there tons of operating efficiencies to be gained? I don't see them," said one executive who did not want to be identified.
But experts also question Illinois Central's ability to survive in an industry increasingly dominated by huge players.
"Illinois Central must feel like there are giants forming up all around it," said one investment banker who has been involved in railroad transactions.
